title: SelfJudge: Faster Speculative Decoding via Self-Supervised Judge Verification
claim: Prior judge-verification methods trade accuracy for speed unevenly across domains; ours keeps near-baseline accuracy with strong speedups on every domain.
layout: 4 panels in 2 pairs, line plot beside bar chart, per dataset
description: Four plot panels are arranged in two pairs, one pair per benchmark. The left pair is titled 'Llama-3.1-8B/Llama-3.2-1B on GSM8K' and the right pair 'on MMLU'. In each pair, a line chart on the left shows average accepted length against gamma (the number of draft tokens per step). It has four series: SD in blue circles, TopK in orange squares, AutoJudge in green triangles, and SelfJudge (ours) in a thick red line with diamonds. A bar chart on the right of each pair shows accuracy for the same four methods, with value labels above the bars. TopK has the longest accepted length but the lowest accuracy: 71.2% on GSM8K and 49.6% on MMLU. On GSM8K, SelfJudge matches SD's 80.5% accuracy. On MMLU, AutoJudge falls to the SD level in accepted length, while SelfJudge stays higher. The eye goes first to the thick red line and the red bars. Panels are labeled (a) to (d).
caption: Inference efficiency and task performance comparison of SD methods on GSM8K (a,b) and MMLU (c,d). AutoJudge shows domain-specific limitations, performing well on mathematical reasoning but poorly on general knowledge tasks, while \proposed maintains consistent performance across both domains. $\gamma$ represents the number of tokens generated by draft model per step.
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by verifying candidate tokens from a draft model against a larger target model. Recent judge decoding boosts this process by relaxing verification criteria by accepting draft tokens that may exhibit minor discrepancies from target model output, but existing methods are restricted by their reliance on human annotations or tasks with verifiable ground truths, limiting generalizability across diverse NLP tasks. We propose SelfJudge, which trains judge verifiers via self-supervision of the target model. Our method measures semantic preservation by assessing whether token-substituted responses preserve the meaning of original responses, enabling automatic verifier training across diverse NLP tasks. Our experiments show SelfJudge achieves superior inference-accuracy trade-offs than judge decoding baselines, offering a broadly applicable solution for faster LLM inference.
